summary:
We created Celestial Archives for the NASA Space Apps "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge: an interactive map and timeline tracking lunar and Martian hardware. The project helps young readers explore what humans left behind on other worlds and the science those instruments accomplished before going quiet.

The map utilizes LROC mosaics for the Moon and Mars Express data for Mars. Moving the timeline reveals location pins for landers, rovers, crash sites, and instrument packages as their missions land. Coordinates, dates, and instrument details are sourced directly from NASA records. If coordinates are missing, they remain unpinned, while sub components share their parent lander's location. Clicking a site opens a middle school friendly story generated by Gemini using verified facts about the hardware's mission, findings, and current resting place.

Though missions end, these artifacts remain indefinitely. Celestial Archives connects verified history with accessible storytelling to keep space history engaging for curious minds.
details:
Project Overview

We built Celestial Archives to track and map historical NASA hardware across the Moon and Mars. On an interactive surface map, color-coded pins mark landers, rovers, impact points, and descent stages. A chronological slider lets you filter these locations by deployment date, though pinpointing exact landing sites sometimes depends on satellite confirmation. Clicking any pin brings up mission metadata: coordinates, landing timestamps, background details, and links to official documentation. A complete directory and reference list back the full collection.

Technical Architecture & Data Integrity

A single database holds every artifact entry. It feeds directly into the main map, the timeline controls, and the search filters.

Historical records often disagree. Rather than forcing a single consensus, we log conflicting source details side by side. For map markers, we rely on LROC imagery whenever available; if reliable spatial data is missing entirely, we leave the entry blank instead of estimating coordinates.

Key Benefits

  • Centralized Access: Brings scattered NASA mission logs together in one place.
  • Interactive Visualization: Turns static archival tables into an interactive, date-filtered map.
  • Full Traceability: Connects each artifact profile directly to its primary source material.
  • Transparent Methodology: Exposes record discrepancies openly rather than smoothing them over.

Future Roadmap

Mapping Lunar and Martian hardware demonstrates what our approach can do. Next, we plan to catalog missions to small bodies like Ceres or Eros alongside deep space probes like Pioneer and Kepler. Down the road, we hope to build out interactive 3D globes, render high-definition terrain data, and publish guided tours of major space exploration milestones.

Technology Stack & Dependencies

  • TypeScript: Primary language across client and server logic.
  • Next.js: Framework providing page routing, API endpoints, and server-side rendering.
  • React: UI library powering the interactive map, timeline, and spatial explorer.
  • Tailwind CSS: Utility-first CSS framework for layout and visual styling.
  • Drizzle ORM & PostgreSQL: Database schema management and query interface.
  • Neon: Serverless PostgreSQL database host.
  • Node.js: JavaScript server runtime environment.
  • Vercel: Deployment platform and cloud hosting provider.
  • NASA NSSDCA Master Catalog: Primary data source for dates, coordinates, and scientific payload metadata.

The site runs in any modern browser without extra setup. As noted in our project submission, we used AI tools to draft initial outlines and code structure.
